input.add_to_description: Day 10 ~5 AM: Wren holds Corvin's quay map, a ring of three keys (brass, iron, tiny bent) and a note: keeper sleeps till dawn bell; 'H.' watches the east door. Wren kept these from the arbiter for now.

entries.text: notebook: updated The Wick-House

You wipe the ink from your boots, pocket the map, the keys and the note, and bolt the door. Your reasoning is sound. Hale is under lock in Thornhallow, so an "H." who watches doors in Saltmarsh is someone else, or someone who answers to him. And a hall with a forger in its cellar may have friends of his in it.

Bess sends up a hot supper of fish pie and bread, which costs three silver. Kit takes the first watch on a stool against the door, with her sword across her knees. You sleep. The night passes without a knock or a creak on the stair, and nothing comes through the walls but the slap of the tide and the odd gull.

The long rest has done its work. You have all 17 hit points, all three spell slots, and Bardic Inspiration back at three. Kit is at full strength too. The exhaustion has eased by one level on both of you, so you are at level 1 now: disadvantage on ability checks remains, but your speed is back to normal.

It is five in the morning on Day 10, and the sky over the estuary is going from black to slate. The dawn bell hasn't rung. Down the quay lies the old building circled in red on Corvin's map, and somewhere near its east door a man named only H. may be watching.

What does Wren do?

sheet.name: Wren Ashgrove
sheet.opening: Wren Ashgrove, a half-elf bard of about nineteen with a quick grin and a sharper tongue, arrives at dusk in the river-market town of Marrowford, a few weeks after fleeing the caravan of her mentor Corvin Tallowmere. She was raised by him as a storyteller's apprentice, and she left in the night at a river crossing with his ledger of forged tales sold to nobles (its pages now hidden in the binding of her road-psalter), a few of his best forgeries, and a head start. She carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, a gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers whom Corvin worshipped only as cover; it holds a curl of yellowed parchment in an unknown hand that may be a true blessing or another forgery. She does not know if Corvin has sent anyone after her. Her ideal: stories should be free, and truth is whatever people can be made to believe. Her bond: find the nobles Corvin cheated and decide whether to expose him or quietly fix what he did. Her flaw: she can't resist a secret, and she lies even when the truth would serve her better. She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. Open on Wren in the square, with the choice of how to approach the wagon and the page, and a locked iron-bound strongbox on the wagon's tailboard that she itches to poke at.

input.add_to_description: Day 9 night: Wren holds Corvin's cache map (Wick-House circled at the seaward end of the quay), three keys, and a note: 'The keeper sleeps till dawn bell. H. watches the east door.' H. is unidentified (Wren doubts it is Master Hale, held in Thornhallow). Wren plans to scout it before the dawn bell on Day 10.

entries.text: notebook: updated The Wick-House

Bess sends up a hot supper of fish stew and bread, and you eat it with the packet spread on the blanket. You wipe the ink off your boots, fold the map into your psalter, and string the three keys on a cord around your neck. The brass one is heavy and plain, the iron one is old, and the tiny bent one looks like it was made for a lock nobody would think to guard.

You keep it all from the arbiter for now. You tell Kit why, and she says only, "Friends in the hall. Aye. Could be." Then she takes the chair against the bolted door with her sword across her knees, and you lie down.

The night passes quietly. The tide mutters under the quay, the gulls go silent, and no one tries the latch. You and Kit swap watches without a word. When you wake, you are mended. Your hit points and spell slots are full, and Bardic Inspiration is back at three. The long rest has taken one level of exhaustion off each of you, so you're both at level 1 now. You still have disadvantage on ability checks, but your speed is whole again.

It's just before four on the morning of Day 10, and the window is black. The dawn bell is a couple of hours off. The quay is yours to scout in the dark, if you'd like to be there first.

You wake rested. The long rest has restored your hit points, all three spell slots and your Bardic Inspiration. Through the window the quay is wet and nearly empty: a few fishwives laying out baskets, a gull on a bollard, and at the seaward end a small, old, low building with a crooked lamp over its door. That's the Wick-House. Corvin's map put the keeper asleep until the bell and "H." at the east door.

Corvin's statement is with the hall, and he's still under guard in the cellar. You haven't told the arbiter about the packet.

The sheet and the clock now agree with what follows.

You wipe the worst of the ink from your boots and pocket the map, the three keys and the note. "H.," you say. "It can't be Hale. He's in a cellar at Thornhallow." Kit shrugs. A man like Hale has friends, and so does the smile that follows him. You keep the packet to yourself, since the hall may leak as easily as any other.

You bolt the door and set Kit on the first watch. Bess sends up a hot supper of fish pie and bread, and you eat all of it, because the rest won't mend you without it. Then you sleep.

The night passes without a knock, a creak or a whisper on the stair. Kit wakes you, or you wake her, somewhere in the small hours, and the watch changes hands without a word. By the time the window greys you've slept your full eight hours. Your hit points are full, your three spell slots are back, and Bardic Inspiration stands at three. Kit is whole too.

The exhaustion is not what it was. A night's sleep and a full stomach have taken one level off both of you, so you're at level 1: disadvantage on ability checks, but your speed is back to normal. It's a quarter to five on Day 10, an hour or so before the dawn bell. Outside, the quay is grey and quiet, with the tide sucking at the pilings and the first gulls waking.

Corvin's note said the keeper sleeps until the dawn bell and that H. watches the east door. The map shows the Wick-House near the seaward end of the quay, with the three keys on your ring: one brass, one iron, one small and bent. What does Wren do?

features: Darkvision: You have superior vision in dark and dim conditions. You can see in dim light within 60 feet of you as if it were bright light, and in darkness as if it were dim light. You cannot discern color in darkness, only shades of gray.
Fey Ancestry: You have advantage on saving throws against being charmed, and magic cannot put you to sleep.
Skill Versatility: You gain proficiency in two skills of your choice.

Bardic Inspiration (d6): You can inspire others through stirring words or music. To do so, you use a bonus action on your turn to choose one creature other than yourself within 60 feet of you who can hear you. That creature gains one Bardic Inspiration die, a d6. Once within the next 10 minutes, the creature can roll the die and add the number rolled to one ability check, attack roll, or saving throw it makes. The creature can wait until after it rolls the d20 before deciding to use the Bardic Inspiration die, but must decide before the GM says whether the roll succeeds or fails. Once the Bardic Inspiration die is rolled, it is lost. A creature can have only one Bardic Inspiration die at a time. You can use this feature a number of times equal to your Charisma modifier (a minimum of once). You regain any expended uses when you finish a long rest.  Your Bardic Inspiration die changes when you reach certain levels in this class. The die becomes a d8 at 5th level, a d10 at 10th level, and a d12 at 15th level. At level 2: Bardic Inspiration die d6.
Jack of All Trades: Starting at 2nd level, you can add half your proficiency bonus, rounded down, to any ability check you make that doesn't already include your proficiency bonus.

Song of Rest (d6): Beginning at 2nd level, you can use soothing music or oration to help revitalize your wounded allies during a short rest. If you or any friendly creatures who can hear your performance regain hit points at the end of the short rest by spending one or more Hit Dice, each of those creatures regains an extra 1d6 hit points.  The extra hit points increase when you reach certain levels in this class: to 1d8 at 9th level, to 1d10 at 13th level, and to 1d12 at 17th level. At level 2: extra 1d6 hit points.

Shelter of the Faithful (Acolyte): As an acolyte, you command the respect of those who share your faith, and you can perform the religious ceremonies of your deity. You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

spellcasting.notes: Spells known are fixed until a level-up.
